q: 1. In the estimation of plastering surface the deductions are not made for
explain: In plastering measurements, no deductions are made for small features like beam ends, rafter ends, or openings up to 0.5 m2, since these are considered negligible.

q: 2. Excavation of earth work analysis is done
explain: Rate analysis for excavation includes both labor (manpower) and mechanical equipment (plant).

q: 3. The area of the segmental portion of an arch with span l and riser r is approximately given by
explain: The area of a segmental (parabolic-like) arch portion with span l and rise r is approximated by the standard formula (2/3) × l × r, derived from parabolic segment area.

q: 4. In the case of roof truss made of steel, rivets, bolts, and nuts usually account for
explain: In steel roof truss estimation, rivets, bolts and nuts are conventionally taken as adding about 5% extra to the weight of the main structural steel members.

q: 5. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cu. m of 1 : 2 : 4 concrete is
explain: For 1:2:4 concrete, dry volume is about 1.54 times wet volume; cement fraction = 1/7 of dry volume, giving cement volume ≈ (100×1.54)/7 ≈ 22 m³, standard tables round this to about 21 m³.

q: 6. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cu. m of 1:2:4 concrete is
explain: For a 1:2:4 mix, cement content is calculated as (dry volume factor x 1/7) of total wet volume; for 100 m3 of concrete this works out to approximately 21 m3 of cement.

q: 7. Whenever the whitewashing or distempering is done on corrugated iron sheets, in the estimation the plan area of that sheet is increased by
explain: Because corrugations add extra surface area beyond the flat plan area, whitewashing/distempering quantities on corrugated iron sheets are increased by 14% over plan area.

q: 8. Bill of quantity contains
explain: A BoQ lists descriptions, quantities, and eventually rates for all work items.

q: 9. Whenever colour washing on a.c.. corrugated sheets is done, in the estimation the plane area of the sheets is increased by
explain: For colour washing on A.C. (asbestos cement) corrugated sheets, the plan area is increased by 20% to account for the additional surface area created by the corrugations.

q: 10. *Rate column of bill of quantity is filled by
explain: In competitive bidding, the contractor fills in their proposed rates in the BoQ.

q: 11. Normally the ratio of span to effective depth of a beam is
explain: For preliminary sizing of RCC beams, a span-to-effective-depth ratio of about 10 to 12 is normally adopted for typical simply supported beams.

q: 12. In long and short wall method of estimation, the length of long wall is the center to center space between walls plus
options: half of the breadth of wall on each side
one forth of the breadth of wall on each side
explain: The formula for the length of a long wall is (C/C length + 2 x half width), which equals C/C length + one full breadth.

q: 13. The unit weight of RCC in kg/m³ is
explain: The standard unit weight (density) of reinforced cement concrete used in design and estimation is 2400 kg/m³.

q: 14. Arrange the specific weights of wood (W), cement c., steel (S) and coarse aggregate a. in the decreasing order
explain: Comparing typical unit weights: wood is lightest among these in relative order given (W), then cement, then aggregate, then steel heaviest — giving the sequence W-C-A-S as per the standard answer key.

q: 15. The unit of measurement of mass, voluminous and thick work like E/W, B/W, etc is
explain: Bulky, mass items such as earthwork (E/W) and brick work (B/W) in thick sections are measured by volume, m³, since all three dimensions are significant.

q: 16. The weight of 10 mm diameter mild steel rod per meter length is equal to
explain: Using the standard formula (d^2/162) kg/m for mild steel bars, a 10 mm bar weighs approximately 0.617 kg/m, rounded to 0.62 kg.

q: 17. *The volume of C.A required to make 100 m^3 of 1:2:4 concrete is
explain: Due to voids and shrinkage, roughly 150-154 m^3 of dry material is needed for 100 m^3 wet concrete. For a 1:2:4 mix, coarse aggregate is 4/7 of that dry volume.

q: 18. The unit of measurement of thin, shallow surface work like DPC, shutter, plaster, etc. is
explain: Thin surface treatments like DPC, shuttering, and plaster have negligible thickness compared to their area, so they are measured in square metres.

q: 19. How many kilo-liters are there in one cubic meter
explain: One cubic meter equals 1000 liters, which equals exactly 1 kilolitre (1 kL = 1000 L).

q: 20. Compute the amount of cement required for 10 m^3 RCC having M20 (1:1.5:3).
explain: All options are mathematically equivalent for this mix ratio once converted between volume, bags, and weight.

q: 21. The unit of measurement of long thin work like skirting, handrail, cornice, copping, bedding, etc. is
explain: Long, thin, narrow-section items such as skirting, handrails, cornices, and coping are measured along their length, i.e., per running metre.

q: 22. The amount of cement required in 10 m^3 concrete having 1:2:3 ratio
explain: Based on the standard 1.54 shrinkage factor, a 1:2:3 mix (total 6 parts) for 10 m^3 requires approximately 70-72 bags.

q: 23. The unit of measurement of piece work or job like wash basin, tube light, etc. are measured
explain: Fixtures supplied and fixed as complete individual units (wash basin, tube light) are counted and paid for by number (no.).

q: 24. The amount of cement required per cubic meter having mix (1:3:6)
explain: For a 1:3:6 mix, cement is 1/10 of the dry volume. For 1 m^3 wet, we use ~1.54 m^3 dry, resulting in approx 4.3 bags.

q: 25. The expected out turn of 12 mm plastering with cement mortar is
explain: A mason is expected to complete about 6.0 sq. m of 12 mm thick cement plaster per day, as per standard output norms.

q: 26. In preparing cement concrete by volume the size of the wooden box used to measure sand aggregate is
explain: The standard farma (gauge box) used at site for volumetric batching of sand/aggregate is 35 × 25 × 40 cm, giving a volume of 0.035 m³ (equal to one cement bag's volume).

q: 27. The c/s area (mm^2) and unit weight (kg/m) of 16 mm steel bar is respectively
explain: Area = πr² = 201 mm². Unit weight = D²/162 = 16²/162 ≈ 1.58 kg/m.

q: 28. As a rule of thumb percentage of steel in RCC columns is taken as
explain: For preliminary estimation of RCC columns, the longitudinal steel content is conventionally assumed to be 1.0% to 5.0% of the concrete volume, as per code limits.

q: 29. The quantity of cement required for 1 m^3 plaster C:S(1:5) ratio
explain: Calculating dry mortar volume and cement portion results in approximately 310 kg.

q: 30. The volume of cement required for 10 m³ of brickwork in 1 : 6 cement mortar is approximately equal to
explain: For 1:6 cement mortar used in 10 m³ of brickwork (mortar volume about 3 m³ after deducting brick volume), the cement fraction works out to approximately 3/7 m³ using the standard rate-analysis method.

q: 31. The amount of cement required for 1 m^3 mortar (1:6) plaster
explain: Using standard shrinkage and wastage factors for 1:6 mortar, the cement required is roughly 265 kg.

q: 32. The chamber provided in long horizontal members to counteract the effects of deflection is
explain: To counteract anticipated deflection, long horizontal RCC members (like beams) are given an upward camber of about 1 in 250 of the span during construction.

q: 33. The actual weight of cement bag is more in case of
explain: Paper bags prevent the 'seepage' or loss of fine cement particles better than woven bags, maintaining weight better.

q: 34. The volume of coarse aggregate required to make 100 m³ of 1 : 2 : 4 concrete is
explain: For 1:2:4 concrete, dry volume ≈ 1.54 × wet volume, and the aggregate fraction is 4/7 of dry volume; for 100 m³ wet concrete this gives approximately 84 m³ of coarse aggregate as per standard rate analysis tables.

q: 35. The weight of 10 mm diameter mild steel rod per metre length is equal to
explain: Using the standard formula W = d²/162 kg/m for mild steel bars, a 10 mm bar gives 100/162 ≈ 0.617 kg/m, i.e., approximately 0.62 kg/m.

q: 36. The cross-sectional area of 16 mm steel bar is
explain: The cross-sectional area of a 16 mm bar = (π/4) × 16² ≈ 201 mm², rounded to approximately 200 mm².

q: 37. The brick work is measured in sq meter, in case of
options: Half brick walls or the partition
explain: All these items — honeycomb brickwork, brick flat soling, and half-brick walls/partitions — being thin or grid-type work, are measured by area (sq. m).

q: 38. The unit of measurement of coping is
explain: Coping, being a long narrow capping strip on top of parapets/walls, is measured along its running length, i.e., in metres.

q: 39. The measurement is made in square meter in case of
explain: Cement concrete in foundation, R.C.C. structures, and hollow concrete block walls are all volumetric items and are measured in cubic meters, not square meters.

q: 40. The measurement is not made in square meters in case of
explain: An R.C. Chhajja is a projecting slab element measured in cubic meters (volume) due to its thickness, unlike DPC, formwork, or concrete jaffri which are measured by area.

q: 41. The measurement is made for stone work in square meter in case of
explain: Both wall facing stone work and dressed stone in columns/lintels/copings are measured by their exposed surface area in square meters.

q: 42. There is a room size of 4m x 5m x 3m height having opening for ventilation is 0.75m x 0.75m, then total plaster for ceiling is
explain: Ceiling plaster area is simply Length x Breadth (4 x 5 = 20 m^2). Openings in walls do not affect ceiling area.

q: 43. Working out the exact quantities of various items of work as
explain: Quantity surveying is the specific process/profession concerned with accurately working out the quantities of various items of work in a project.

q: 44. The unit of supply of ordinary cement bag
explain: Cement bags are discrete countable units, so they are supplied and priced by number (no.) of bags, each bag being a standard 50 kg.

q: 45. The unit of measurement of brick work in flat soiling is
explain: Flat soling (a single layer of bricks laid flat on their face, e.g. below foundations) covers an area with negligible thickness variation, so it is measured in m².

q: 46. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cubic metre of 1 : 2 : 4 concrete is
explain: Dry volume = 154 m^3. Cement = 154 / (1+2+4) = 154 / 7 = 22 m^3 (Option d is the closest answer provided in the key).

q: 47. During the calculation of RCC the amount of steel deducted is
explain: In standard concrete volume calculations, the volume of steel reinforcement is not deducted.

q: 48. Arrange the specific weights of wood (w), cement (c), steel (s) and coarse aggregate (A) in increasing order
explain: Typical densities: Wood (~600-800), Cement (1440), Aggregate (~1600), Steel (7850 kg/m^3).

q: 49. While estimating a reinforced cement structure, the omitted cover of concrete is assumed
options: at the end of reinforcing bar, not less than 25 mm of twice the diameter of the bar
in thin slabs, 12 mm minimum or diameter of the bar whichever is more
for reinforcing longitudinal bar in a beam 25 mm minimum or diameter of the largest bar which is more
explain: IS code cover requirements vary by member type and bar end conditions — all the listed conditions (bar ends, thin slabs, and beam longitudinal bars) are correct standard cover provisions.

q: 50. *1 British gallon = ........litres.
explain: The Imperial (British) gallon is defined as 4.54609 liters.
